title: The review of a quiet-room demonstration
public_context: A case narrative from a fictional college learning-access office concerns a studio assessment and a student's request about its format. The file brings together an instructor's account, a review panel's notes and an assessment sheet within a familiar educational setting. It is one file in a larger office archive.
source_title: Learning Access Office case narrative 17, prepared for the studio faculty
source_text:
When Tavi Ren enrolled in the third-year sound studio, the final assessment was described as a live explanation of a finished installation. Ren asked to demonstrate the work in the quiet room instead of the crowded gallery, where the open mixing desk and rotating audience made it difficult to follow the sequence of sounds. The instructor, Hal Orin, initially thought the request concerned only volume. Ren's note explained that the order mattered: a low pulse had to be heard before a metal rattle, or the rattle seemed to begin the piece.

The review panel met with Ren, Orin and the studio technician. They listened to a six-minute recording made in the quiet room, then examined a cue sheet Ren had marked with arrows. The recording contained the same seven sound events as the gallery version, but the panel could not tell from the recording alone which switches Ren had operated. The technician showed a photograph of the labeled desk, and Ren replayed the first minute while naming each control before touching it. The panel asked that the demonstration include both the audible sequence and a visible trace of the operator's choices.

The faculty agreed to let Ren present in the quiet room, with two reviewers in the room and one watching through a glass partition. The panel did not waive the explanation requirement, and it did not ask the technician to operate the desk. Ren would speak the cue names while changing the switches, then leave the installation running once without commentary so the reviewers could hear the complete sequence. The agreed format was written on the assessment sheet and signed by Ren and Orin. The decision resolved where and how the work would be shown, but it did not record a mark.

At the later review, Ren named the controls and played the piece. Orin's note says the panel accepted the sequence as complete and asked Ren to clarify why the rattle entered after the low pulse. Ren answered that the pulse established the room's imagined size; the panel's minutes record the question but not a verbatim answer. The panel chair tapped the signed sheet and asked the clerk to place the case on the next faculty agenda. Orin returned the recording to the quiet-room cabinet; Ren waited beside the door while the reviewers filed out, then folded the cue sheet into the folder. The panel's question about the low pulse remained in the margin.
